fetched_contents.text: Validity of British Thoracic Society guidance (the CRB-65 rule) for predicting the severity of pneumonia in general practice: systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background The CRB-65 score is a clinical prediction rule that grades the severity of community-acquired pneumonia in terms of 30-day mortality. Aim The study sought to validate CRB-65 and assess its clinical value in community and hospital settings. Design of study Systematic review and meta-analysis of validation studies of CRB-65. Method Medline (1966 to June 2009), Embase (1988 to November 2008), British Nursing Index (BNI) and PsychINFO were searched, using a diagnostic accuracy search filter combined with subject-specific terms. The derived (index) rule was used as a predictive model and applied to all validation studies. Comparison was made between the observed and predicted number of deaths stratified by risk group (low, intermediate, and high) and setting of care (community or hospital). Pooled results are presented as risk ratios (RRs) in terms of over-prediction (RR>1) or under-prediction (RR<1) of 30-day mortality. Results Fourteen validation studies totalling 397 875 patients are included. CRB-65 performs well in hospitalised patients, particularly in those classified as intermediate (RR 0.91, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.71 to 1.17) or high risk (RR 1.01, 95% CI = 0.87 to 1.16). In community settings, CRB-65 over-predicts the probability of 30-day mortality across all strata of predicted risk, low (RR 9.41, 95% CI = 1.75 to 50.66), intermediate (RR 4.84, 95% CI = 2.61 to 8.69), and high (RR 1.58, 95% CI = 0.59 to 4.19). Conclusion CRB-65 performs well in stratifying severity of pneumonia and resultant 30-day mortality in hospital settings. In community settings, CRB-65 appears to over-predict the probability of 30-day mortality across all strata of predicted risk. Caution is needed when applying CRB-65 to patients in general practice. Keywords: general practice, meta-analysis, pneumonia, prognosis, severity of illness index INTRODUCTION Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) has an annual incidence of 5–11 per 1000, accounting for 5–12% of all cases of adult lower respiratory tract infection managed by GPs.1 Appropriate management for patients with suspected CAP must be determined by GPs at initial presentation, particularly with regard to whether or not to manage a patient in the community or refer them to hospital.2 The proportion of adults with CAP who require hospital admission in the UK varies between 22% and 42%.1 This proportion varies in other countries, possibly due to differing structures of primary and secondary healthcare systems.1 Furthermore, of those initially managed in the community, less than 10% subsequently require hospital admission. At the other end of the severity spectrum, between 5% and 10% of patients admitted to hospital require management in an intensive care unit (ICU).1 Severity assessment in patients with suspected CAP plays a key part in planning appropriate management in both community and hospital settings, as the setting of care has an impact on the level of treatment given to the patient as well as the overall costs of treatment.1 The CRB-65 score (Figure 1) is a clinical prediction rule derived to determine the severity of CAP and to aid the physician in arranging appropriate treatment.3 It ranks patients into strata of low, intermediate, or high risk of mortality based on four criteria (new-onset confusion; respiratory rate ≥30/minutes; systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≤60 mmHg; and age ≥65 years), in terms of estimated mortality risk (Figure 1). It is also forms the basis of an algorithm to determine the most appropriate site of care.1 The CRB-65 score is a simplified version of the CURB-65 rule (inclusion of urea estimation: raised >7 mmol/l), and has been advocated for use in community settings as its criteria depend on clinical assessment (history and physical examination) alone.4 How this fits in The CRB-65 rule grades the severity of community-acquired pneumonia in terms of 30-day mortality risk. Although it is intended for use in the community setting the majority of validation studies are hospital based. This systematic review suggests that the CRB-65 rule performs well in hospital settings but may over-predict the probability of 30-day mortality in community settings, and should be used with caution. There are specific methodological standards that are applied to clinical prediction rules before their use in clinical practice can be recommended. Ideally, a rule undergoes three steps: derivation, narrow and broad validation, and impact analysis (randomised controlled trial assessing its effectiveness and cost-effectiveness).5–7 The CRB-65 rule has been validated extensively in separate studies, although for a clinical prediction rule specifically intended for community use there have been few validation studies performed wholly in primary care.1,8 As clinical prediction rules may not perform well in practice because of deficiencies in the development methods or because of differences between the original sample and the validation sample, it is good practice to assess their validity across a broad range of eligible patient groups.9 The aim of this study was to perform a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of validation studies of CRB-65, to determine its accuracy in predicting 30-day mortality and assess how well it performs in community and hospital settings. fetched_contents.text: Guidelines for the Evaluation and Treatment of Pneumonia Abstract Pneumonia is a common cause of respiratory infection, accounting for more than 800,000 hospitalizations in the United States annually. Presenting symptoms of pneumonia are typically cough, pleuritic chest pain, fever, fatigue, and loss of appetite. Children and the elderly have different presenting features of pneumonia, which include headache, nausea, abdominal pain, and absence of one or more of the prototypical symptoms. Knowledge of local bacterial pathogens and their antibiotic susceptibility and resistance profiles is the key for effective pharmacologic selection and treatment of pneumonia. Keywords: Pneumonia, Ventilator-associated, Community-acquired, Pediatric, Antibiotic resistance, Microbial pathogens Key points * • Pneumonia is a common respiratory infection and warrants careful consideration of antibiotic initiation and choice, along with knowledge of local antibiotic resistance patterns. * • Community-acquired pneumonia afflicts all age groups and although not always bacterial in origin, is clinically versatile, depending on its cause. * • Nonresolving pneumonia may be because of less common pathogens, or feature other conditions, and requires more detailed investigation. * • Pediatric pneumonia is also common, and first-line treatment is still amoxicillin, followed closely by cephalosporins or macrolides. * • Other categories of pneumonia, including mechanically induced (ventilator) or travel/geriatric pneumonia, benefit from astute clinical acumen, proper history and physical examination, and knowledge of microbial causes. Introduction Pneumonia is a leading cause of hospitalization among both adults and children in the United States, accounting for more than 800,000 hospitalizations and more than 400,000 emergency department visits in 2014.1, 2 It is among the most expensive conditions treated in US hospitals with national aggregate costs of $9.5 billion in 2013.3 A causal pathogen is often not identified. A 2015 prospective, multi-center study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identified a responsible pathogen in only 38% of cases of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in adults requiring hospitalization.4 CAP is an infection of the lung parenchyma that is acquired outside of hospitals or extended-care facilities.5 Viral pathogens were identified in 27% of cases and bacterial pathogens in 14% of cases.5 In adults of all ages, human rhinovirus and influenza were the most frequently identified viruses.5 Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common causal bacterium. Staphylococcus aureus and Enterobacteriaceae were significantly more common among patients requiring intensive care unit (ICU) level care.4 Other bacteria identified in CAP include Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae.5 Less common bacterial causes include Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Legionella sp, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. When to step up care and what escalation options are appropriate

The evidence here points to a clear escalation logic: the patient should move from observation or outpatient treatment to hospitalization, ICU admission, or transfer when clinical deterioration, worsening respiratory failure, or signs of severe CAP are present. The main escalation trigger is not just a single abnormal sign but a progression of symptoms and findings that increase suspicion of severe disease.

Clinical signs or lab findings that indicate escalation include worsening respiratory failure, shortness of breath, febrile illness, and abnormal vital signs. One source notes that patients who are short of breath, febrile, and in respiratory distress need to be managed more urgently [N2-R3]. Another source explicitly states that interventions to increase outpatient treatment of mild pneumonia were safe and effective, which implies that patients who do not fit that mild profile are more likely to need escalation [N2-R1]. The evidence also highlights that approximately 10% of outpatients do not respond to antibiotic therapy and require hospitalization [N2-R5], and that complicated pneumonia can require prolonged therapy once fever is gone [N6-R1]. That suggests that failure to improve is itself a strong escalation signal.

When to consider ICU admission or transfer is tied to the severity of respiratory failure and the need for intensive management. One source states that a pneumonia patient can be safely transferred from the ICU to the ward when they no longer meet severe CAP criteria and have achieved stability [N4-R4]. Another source notes that patients initially admitted to a non-ICU setting but later requiring ICU transfer have higher mortality than patients with equivalent illness treated in the ICU [N4-R5]. This is important because it shows that ICU admission is not simply a default step for all severe pneumonia cases; it is reserved for patients whose condition deteriorates enough to justify intensive care. The same source also states that the main reason for transfer to ICU was worsening respiratory failure [N4-R3], which reinforces that ICU admission should be guided by progressive respiratory compromise rather than mere suspicion.

How to decide between observation, outpatient treatment, or hospitalization depends on the patient’s overall risk profile and response to initial management. The evidence suggests that outpatient treatment is appropriate for patients who are stable and fit the criteria for mild disease, whereas hospitalization is needed when there is concern about deterioration or when outpatient treatment fails. One source says that most patients respond to outpatient antibiotic therapy for 5 to 7 days, but patients who do not respond may need hospitalization [N2-R3]. Another source says that CURB-65 is used to help determine inpatient versus outpatient treatment [N1-F2], and that CURB-65 score of 0 or 1 corresponds to outpatient care, while a score of 2 is intermediate and a score of ≥3 corresponds to inpatient admission [N1-F2]. The broader context also indicates that community-based management is possible for many patients, but that patients initially managed in the community who later require ICU transfer have higher mortality [N4-R5], so hospitalization should be considered more carefully when the patient is not clearly stable or when the risk of deterioration is high.

A practical limitation of this escalation logic is that the evidence is not entirely standardized across all settings. One source notes that CURB-65 may over-predict 30-day mortality in community settings, which means the score should be used with caution rather than as an absolute decision rule [N1-F1]. Another source emphasizes that mortality prediction tools such as CURB-65 and CRB-65 should be used to supplement, rather than replace, clinical judgment [N7-R5]. This matters because escalation decisions should not rely solely on a score; they should also consider the patient’s overall condition, comorbidities, and response to treatment.

Overall, the practical message is: escalate care when there is worsening respiratory failure, fever, shortness of breath, or failure to respond to initial treatment; consider ICU admission when respiratory failure worsens or when the patient is at high risk of deterioration; and choose hospitalization over outpatient treatment when the patient is unstable, has a high predicted risk, or does not meet criteria for mild disease [N2-R3][N2-R1][N2-R5][N4-R3][N4-R5][N1-F2].

Follow-up and reassessment after pneumonia treatment

After pneumonia treatment begins, follow-up should focus on monitoring clinical improvement, reassessing the need for continued treatment, and identifying signs that the patient is not improving. The evidence here supports a structured follow-up approach rather than a one-time checkup.

What to monitor during follow-up includes clinical stability, resolution of fever, and improvement in respiratory symptoms. One source states that complicated pneumonia will require a minimum of 2 weeks of therapy once lack of fever is confirmed and may be extended for up to 4 weeks [N6-R1]. This means that fever clearance is a key milestone in deciding whether treatment can be adjusted. The same source also says that the switch from one antibiotic to another should be based on clinical response and microbiological results [N8-R1], which is important because follow-up should be guided by both clinical and laboratory evidence.

When to repeat imaging or lab tests depends on the patient’s response and clinical context. One source notes that follow-up chest X-rays may be considered at 6 weeks after discharge in people with risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease, or when there are persisting symptoms [N6-R2]. This suggests that repeated imaging should be used selectively for patients with ongoing concern or risk factors, not routinely. The evidence also supports that follow-up should include safety assessment, medication management, and medical reevaluation after severe pneumonia or acute respiratory failure [N6-F4], which implies that reassessment should be comprehensive rather than limited to a single test.

When to reassess treatment and escalate care depends on whether the patient is improving. The evidence states that approximately 10% of outpatients do not respond to antibiotic therapy and require hospitalization [N2-R5], and that most patients respond to outpatient antibiotic therapy for 5 to 7 days [N2-R3]. This means that failure to improve within a reasonable time is a strong reason to reassess. The same source also says that for outpatients who reach clinical stability, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate [N6-R3], which suggests that reassessment should include both clinical stability and the duration of treatment. If the patient is not improving, the evidence implies that escalation is needed, including possible hospitalization or further diagnostic workup.

The broader context also supports the idea that follow-up should be tailored to the patient’s risk profile. One source emphasizes that CURB-65 and CRB-65 should be used to supplement rather than replace clinical judgment [N7-R5], which means follow-up decisions should remain clinical and not solely algorithmic. Another source notes that patients initially managed in the community who later require ICU transfer have higher mortality than equivalent ICU-treated patients [N4-R5], reinforcing that follow-up should remain vigilant for deterioration even after initial improvement.

In short, follow-up should monitor clinical improvement and fever clearance, repeat imaging or lab tests selectively when there are risk factors or persistent symptoms, and reassess treatment if the patient is not improving. Escalation should be guided by clinical stability, duration of treatment, and response to therapy [N6-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N6-R2][N6-F4].

How to quickly triage pneumonia using CRB-65 and CURB-65

Both CRB-65 and CURB-65 are severity prediction rules designed to help clinicians stratify patients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and decide whether inpatient or outpatient care is appropriate, but they differ in their components and intended use.

CRB-65 is simpler and intended for use in community settings. It includes four criteria: new-onset confusion; respiratory rate ≥30/min; systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≤60 mmHg; and age ≥65 years [N1-F1]. The source says CRB-65 is a simplified version of CURB-65 and has been advocated for use in community settings because its criteria depend on clinical assessment alone [N1-F1]. It also says that CRB-65 is a clinical prediction rule that grades severity of CAP in terms of 30-day mortality and is used to aid the physician in arranging appropriate treatment [N1-F1]. A separate source notes that CURB-65 is a five-point score estimating mortality of CAP to help determine inpatient versus outpatient treatment [N1-F2].

CURB-65 is slightly more complex because it includes urea. The CURB-65 score ranges from 0 to 5, with points assigned for confusion, urea >7 mmol/l, respiratory rate ≥30/min, blood pressure ≤90 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F2]. The same source provides thresholds: 0 or 1 corresponds to outpatient care, 2 corresponds to intermediate risk, and ≥3 corresponds to inpatient admission with consideration for ICU admission for scores of 4 or 5 [N1-F2]. Another source describes CURB-65 as a simple tool to aid clinical decision-making in stratifying patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups [N7-R4].

The threshold values that separate low-risk from higher-risk patients are therefore different for the two scores. For CRB-65, the evidence does not give a simple numerical cutoff in the provided material, but it does say that CRB-65 separates patients into low, intermediate, and high risk based on the four criteria [N1-F1]. For CURB-65, the cutoffs are explicit: 0 or 1 is outpatient, 2 is intermediate, and ≥3 is inpatient [N1-F2]. The evidence also states that patients with the highest CURB-65 score of 5 had higher mortality than those in the highest PSI-HR risk class [N1-R3], suggesting that higher scores correspond to higher mortality risk.

When each score is more appropriate and what clinical context matters is an important distinction. CRB-65 is more appropriate for community settings because it uses only clinical assessment and does not require laboratory testing such as urea measurement [N1-F1][N7-R3]. CURB-65 is more appropriate when urea is available and when more detailed severity stratification is needed, because it includes urea and can better separate risk groups [N1-F2][N7-R4]. The evidence also notes that CURB-65 may over-predict 30-day mortality in community settings and should be used with caution [N1-F1]. That matters because it means CURB-65 is best used where laboratory data are available and where more precise risk stratification is clinically useful, while CRB-65 is better suited for settings where laboratory tests may not be routinely available.

Overall, the practical difference is that CRB-65 is simpler and intended for community use, while CURB-65 is more sensitive and better suited for hospital or settings where urea can be measured [N1-F1][N1-F2][N7-R3]. The choice between them should depend on the clinical context, availability of laboratory data, and the need for precise risk stratification [N7-R5].

How to choose initial antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia

The evidence supports a clear approach to initial antibiotic selection for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP): first-line regimens vary by patient risk, severity, and local resistance patterns, but commonly include beta-lactam/macrolide combinations, fluoroquinolones, or other broad-cover regimens when appropriate. The evidence also indicates that antibiotics should be adjusted based on comorbidities, severity, and response to treatment.

Recommended first-line antibiotic regimens by guideline. The strongest evidence in the provided material is that the ATS/IDSA guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations on initial empiric antibiotic therapy for adult CAP [N3-F3]. The guidelines explicitly address the selection of initial therapy and subsequent management decisions, and they indicate that some recommendations remain unchanged while others have been revised based on new evidence [N3-F3]. Although the provided excerpts do not include the full guideline text, the evidence does show that outpatient CAP is often managed with shorter-course antibiotics once clinical stability is achieved, and that fluoroquinolones or beta-lactam plus macrolide combinations are used for hospitalized patients [N3-R5]. Another source says that previously healthy patients without recent antibiotic use can be treated with doxycycline 100 mg PO BID or amoxicillin 1 gm PO TID [N3-R2], which is useful for low-risk outpatient CAP. A separate source also states that complicated pneumonia may require prolonged therapy once fever is gone [N6-R1], supporting the idea that initial selection must balance coverage and duration.

When to use combination therapy or broader coverage. Combination therapy is appropriate when the patient is at higher risk of severe disease, when local resistance patterns suggest broader coverage is needed, or when the patient is hospitalized. The evidence supports that hospitalized patients may receive fluoroquinolone or beta-lactam plus macrolide therapy [N3-R5]. It also suggests that combination therapy may be used when there is concern about resistant organisms, because one source notes that complicated pneumonia may require extended therapy once fever is confirmed [N6-R1]. Another source notes that MRSA coverage should be added with vancomycin or linezolid if the patient has a history of MRSA or recent IV antibiotics/hospitalization, and that Pseudomonas coverage should be added when appropriate [N8-R2]. This indicates that broader coverage should be guided by comorbidities, recent exposures, and local resistance patterns rather than used routinely.

How to adjust antibiotics based on comorbidities and severity. Adjustment should be based on clinical response, severity, and microbiological results. The evidence says that the switch from one antibiotic to another should be based on clinical response and microbiological results [N8-R1]. It also states that for outpatients who reach clinical stability, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate, with a minimum of 3 days rather than longer courses [N6-R3]. For hospitalized patients, the evidence suggests that treatment duration should be at least 5 days unless MRSA or Pseudomonas is confirmed, in which case the duration may be adjusted [N8-R4]. This means that comorbidities such as MRSA risk, heart failure, or recent hospitalization should increase the likelihood of broader coverage, while clinical stability should allow tapering or shorter courses.

The broader context also supports that antibiotic choice should be guided by local bacterial pathogens and resistance profiles, because one source emphasizes that knowledge of local bacterial pathogens and their antibiotic susceptibility and resistance profiles is key for effective pharmacologic selection [N1-F4]. That means the choice of initial antibiotics should not be one-size-fits-all but should depend on the patient’s risk profile, local epidemiology, and response to treatment.

In summary, the practical recommendations are: use beta-lactam/macrolide combinations or fluoroquinolones as first-line therapy for hospitalized patients, doxycycline or amoxicillin for low-risk outpatient patients, and consider broader coverage when MRSA, Pseudomonas, or other resistant organisms are suspected [N3-F3][N3-R5][N3-R2][N8-R2]. Adjust duration and coverage based on clinical response, severity, and microbiological evidence, and shorten duration when patients reach clinical stability [N6-R3][N8-R1].

Practical implementation and limitations of the triage process

The evidence shows that the triage process using severity scores like CRB-65 and CURB-65 is useful but not perfect. Its practical implementation depends on clear criteria, careful interpretation, and the recognition that scoring alone is not sufficient.

Common pitfalls in scoring and interpretation include over-reliance on the score and misapplication of the score across different settings. The evidence states that CURB-65 may over-predict 30-day mortality in community settings and should be used with caution [N1-F1]. It also says that mortality prediction tools such as CURB-65 and CRB-65 should be used to supplement rather than replace clinical judgment [N7-R5]. This is a major limitation: using the score as a substitute for clinical assessment can lead to incorrect decisions, especially in community settings where the score may over-predict mortality [N1-F1]. Another source notes that CURB-65 is rather more sensitive for determining patients with severe illness, and lacks sensitivity toward other aspects of illness [N7-R2], suggesting that the score may miss some patients who are not clearly severe by the score alone.

How to handle uncertainty or atypical presentations is an important practical issue. The evidence emphasizes that clinical judgment must supplement the score, and that the score is intended to help decide inpatient versus outpatient treatment rather than replace judgment [N7-R5]. For atypical presentations, this means clinicians should not assume the patient fits a standard pattern. One source says that community-acquired pneumonia can be caused by a variety of pathogens, including viral, bacterial, and other organisms, and that the clinical presentation may vary [N1-F4]. Another source says that patients initially managed in the community who later require ICU transfer have higher mortality than those treated in the ICU [N4-R5], which means that uncertainty should prompt more cautious escalation than the score alone would suggest.

What to do if the patient is not improving after treatment is another critical part of triage. The evidence indicates that approximately 10% of outpatients do not respond to antibiotic therapy and require hospitalization [N2-R5], and that most patients respond to outpatient therapy for 5 to 7 days [N2-R3]. It also says that complicated pneumonia may require prolonged therapy once fever is confirmed and may be extended for up to 4 weeks [N6-R1]. The evidence also supports reassessment based on clinical response and microbiological results [N8-R1]. If the patient is not improving, the practical response is to reassess treatment, consider changing antibiotics, and escalate care if needed. One source notes that the switch from one antibiotic to another should be based on clinical response and microbiological results [N8-R1], which means that non-improvement is a strong trigger for reassessment rather than a reason to continue the same regimen indefinitely.

The broader limitations also include the fact that severity scores are based on historical data and may not always reflect current practice or local patterns. # Integrated final answer: how to quickly triage pneumonia using CRB-65 or CURB-65, pick antibiotics, and step up care if needed

## 1) Quick triage using CRB-65 and CURB-65

The two most commonly used severity scores for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) are **CRB-65** and **CURB-65**. Both are intended to help you decide whether the patient is likely to be stable enough for outpatient treatment or needs hospitalization, but they differ in what they measure and where they are best used.

### CRB-65
- **What it measures**: new-onset confusion, respiratory rate ≥30/min, systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≤60 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F1].
- **Why it matters**: CRB-65 is simpler and intended for community settings because it uses only clinical assessment and does not require laboratory testing such as urea [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- **Thresholds and risk groups**: the evidence says CRB-65 separates patients into low, intermediate, and high risk based on those four criteria [N1-F1]. The provided material does not give a single numerical cutoff for low-risk versus higher-risk, so the main point is that higher scores mean higher mortality risk [N1-F1].
- **Best when**: you want a quick, simple rule in community practice and laboratory testing is not readily available [N1-F1][N7-R3].

### CURB-65
- **What it measures**: confusion, urea >7 mmol/l, respiratory rate ≥30/min, blood pressure ≤90 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F2].
- **Why it matters**: CURB-65 is a five-point score that estimates mortality of CAP to help determine inpatient versus outpatient treatment [N1-F2].
- **Thresholds and risk groups**: the cutoffs are explicit: 0 or 1 = outpatient care; 2 = intermediate risk; ≥3 = inpatient admission with consideration for ICU admission for scores of 4 or 5 [N1-F2]. Higher scores also correlate with higher mortality [N1-R3].
- **Best when**: you need a more detailed severity stratification, urea can be measured, and you are in a setting where laboratory data are available [N1-F2][N7-R4].

### Practical difference
- **CRB-65** is simpler and better suited for community use [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- **CURB-65** is more sensitive for severe illness and better suited for hospital or settings where urea is available [N1-F2][N7-R4].
- Both scores should be used to **supplement, not replace, clinical judgment** [N7-R5].

## 2) How to choose initial antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia

The evidence points to a clear evidence-based approach: first-line antibiotics depend on the patient’s risk, severity, and local resistance patterns, but commonly include beta-lactam/macrolide combinations, fluoroquinolones, or other broad-cover regimens when needed.

### Recommended first-line antibiotic regimens
- **Low-risk outpatient CAP**: previously healthy patients without recent antibiotic use can be treated with **doxycycline 100 mg PO BID** or **amoxicillin 1 gm PO TID** [N3-R2].
- **Hospitalized patients**: the guidelines recommend **fluoroquinolone** or **beta-lactam plus macrolide** combinations [N3-R5].
- **General outpatient CAP**: outpatient CAP is often managed with shorter-course antibiotics once clinical stability is achieved [N6-R3].

### When to use combination therapy or broader coverage
- Use **combination therapy** or **broader coverage** when the patient is at higher risk of severe disease, when local resistance patterns suggest broader coverage is needed, or when the patient is hospitalized [N3-F3].
- Add **MRSA coverage** with **vancomycin or linezolid** if the patient has a history of MRSA or recent IV antibiotics/hospitalization [N8-R2].
- Add **Pseudomonas coverage** when appropriate, especially in patients with risk factors or when local epidemiology suggests it [N8-R2].

### How to adjust antibiotics based on comorbidities and severity
- Adjust antibiotics based on **clinical response** and **microbiological results** [N8-R1].
- For outpatients who reach clinical stability, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate, with a minimum of 3 days [N6-R3].
- For complicated pneumonia, therapy should continue for at least 2 weeks once fever is gone and may be extended for up to 4 weeks [N6-R1].
- If MRSA or Pseudomonas is confirmed, adjust duration accordingly [N8-R4].

### Key takeaway
Start with a guideline-based first-line regimen, use combination therapy when needed, and adjust based on severity, comorbidities, and response to treatment [N3-F3][N3-R5][N3-R2][N8-R2].

## 3) When to step up care and what escalation options are appropriate

The evidence supports a clear escalation logic: move from observation or outpatient treatment to hospitalization, ICU admission, or transfer when clinical deterioration, worsening respiratory failure, or failure to respond to treatment occurs.

### Clinical signs or lab findings that indicate escalation
- Shortness of breath, fever, and respiratory distress [N2-R3].
- Abnormal vital signs, especially respiratory failure and worsening respiratory status [N4-R3].
- Failure to improve after initial treatment [N2-R5][N6-R1].

### When to consider ICU admission or transfer
- Consider ICU admission if there is **worsening respiratory failure** or if the patient is at high risk of deterioration [N4-R3].
- Patients initially admitted to a non-ICU setting but later requiring ICU transfer have higher mortality than patients treated in the ICU [N4-R5].
- A pneumonia patient can be safely transferred from the ICU to the ward when they no longer meet severe CAP criteria and have achieved stability [N4-R4].

### How to decide between observation, outpatient treatment, or hospitalization
- Use outpatient care for stable, low-risk patients who meet mild disease criteria [N2-R1][N2-R3].
- Use hospitalization when there is concern about deterioration or when outpatient treatment fails [N2-R5][N4-R5].
- Use ICU admission when respiratory failure worsens or when the patient is at higher risk [N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 4) Practical implementation and limitations of the triage process

The triage process using severity scores like CRB-65 and CURB-65 is useful but not perfect. It works best when used alongside clinical judgment.

### Common pitfalls
- Over-reliance on the score alone can lead to incorrect decisions, especially in community settings [N1-F1].
- CURB-65 may over-predict 30-day mortality in community settings and should be used with caution [N1-F1].
- The score should be used to **supplement, not replace, clinical judgment** [N7-R5].

### How to handle uncertainty or atypical presentations
- Atypical presentations require more cautious escalation than the score alone would suggest [N7-R5].
- Clinical judgment must remain central, especially for patients whose presentation is unusual or does not fit a standard pattern [N7-R5][N4-R5].

### What to do if the patient is not improving after treatment
- If the patient is not improving, reassess treatment, consider changing antibiotics, and escalate care if needed [N6-R1][N8-R1].
- Approximately 10% of outpatients do not respond to antibiotic therapy and require hospitalization [N2-R5].
- Most patients respond to outpatient therapy for 5 to 7 days [N2-R3].

## 5) Follow-up and reassessment after pneumonia treatment

After treatment starts, follow-up should focus on monitoring improvement and determining whether treatment can be adjusted or escalated.

### What to monitor during follow-up
- Clinical improvement and fever clearance [N6-R1].
- Resolution of respiratory symptoms [N6-R2].
- Overall stability and response to treatment [N6-F4].

### When to repeat imaging or lab tests
- Repeat chest X-rays may be considered at 6 weeks after discharge in people with risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease, or when there are persisting symptoms [N6-R2].
- Reassess with safety assessment, medication management, and medical reevaluation after severe pneumonia or acute respiratory failure [N6-F4].

### When to reassess treatment and escalate care
- Reassess treatment if the patient is not improving [N6-R1][N2-R5].
- If clinical stability is reached, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate [N6-R3].
- If the patient is still unstable, consider changing antibiotics and escalating care [N8-R1].

## 6) Summary: quick patient-friendly steps

### Step 1: Triage using CRB-65 or CURB-65
- Use **CRB-65** for a quick, simple community rule [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- Use **CURB-65** for more detailed severity stratification when urea is available [N1-F2][N7-R4].
- Always use the score to **supplement clinical judgment**, not replace it [N7-R5].

### Step 2: Choose initial antibiotics
- Outpatient low-risk CAP: **doxycycline** or **amoxicillin** [N3-R2].
- Hospitalized CAP: **fluoroquinolone** or **beta-lactam plus macrolide** [N3-R5].
- Add broader coverage if there is MRSA, Pseudomonas, or other risk factors [N8-R2].
- Adjust duration and regimen based on clinical response and microbiological results [N8-R1][N6-R3].

### Step 3: Step up care if needed
- Escalate if there is worsening respiratory failure, fever, shortness of breath, or failure to improve [N2-R3][N4-R3][N2-R5].
- Consider ICU admission if respiratory failure worsens or the patient is at high risk [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- Transfer from ICU to ward when the patient stabilizes and no longer meets severe CAP criteria [N4-R4].

### Step 4: Follow up and reassess
- Monitor clinical improvement and fever clearance [N6-R1].
- Repeat imaging or lab tests selectively if there are risk factors or persistent symptoms [N6-R2].
- Reassess treatment if the patient is not improving, and change antibiotics as needed [N6-R1][N8-R1].

## Final practical note

If the patient is not improving after treatment, the evidence clearly says to **reassess treatment and escalate care** rather than continue the same regimen indefinitely [N6-R1][N8-R1]. The main takeaway is: **do not rely on a score alone; use it with clinical judgment, adjust antibiotics when needed, and escalate care when the patient is getting worse or not responding** [N1-F1][N7-R5][N2-R5].

# Integrated final answer: how to quickly triage pneumonia using CRB-65 or CURB-65, pick antibiotics, and step up care if needed

## 1) Quick triage using CRB-65 and CURB-65

The two most commonly used severity scores for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) are **CRB-65** and **CURB-65**. Both are intended to help you decide whether the patient is likely to be stable enough for outpatient treatment or needs hospitalization, but they differ in what they measure and where they are best used.

### CRB-65
- **What it measures**: new-onset confusion, respiratory rate ≥30/min, systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≤60 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F1].
- **Why it matters**: CRB-65 is simpler and intended for community settings because it uses only clinical assessment and does not require laboratory testing such as urea [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- **Thresholds and risk groups**: the evidence says CRB-65 separates patients into low, intermediate, and high risk based on those four criteria [N1-F1]. The provided material does not give a single numerical cutoff for low-risk versus higher-risk, so the main point is that higher scores mean higher mortality risk [N1-F1].
- **Best when**: you want a quick, simple rule in community practice and laboratory testing is not readily available [N1-F1][N7-R3].

### CURB-65
- **What it measures**: confusion, urea >7 mmol/l, respiratory rate ≥30/min, blood pressure ≤90 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F2].
- **Why it matters**: CURB-65 is a five-point score that estimates mortality of CAP to help determine inpatient versus outpatient treatment [N1-F2].
- **Thresholds and risk groups**: the cutoffs are explicit: 0 or 1 = outpatient care; 2 = intermediate risk; ≥3 = inpatient admission with consideration for ICU admission for scores of 4 or 5 [N1-F2]. Higher scores also correlate with higher mortality [N1-R3].
- **Best when**: you need a more detailed severity stratification, urea can be measured, and you are in a setting where laboratory data are available [N1-F2][N7-R4].

### Practical difference
- **CRB-65** is simpler and better suited for community use [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- **CURB-65** is more sensitive for severe illness and better suited for hospital or settings where urea is available [N1-F2][N7-R4].
- Both scores should be used to **supplement, not replace, clinical judgment** [N7-R5].

## 2) How to choose initial antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia

The evidence points to a clear evidence-based approach: first-line antibiotics depend on the patient’s risk, severity, and local resistance patterns, but commonly include beta-lactam/macrolide combinations, fluoroquinolones, or other broad-cover regimens when needed.

### Recommended first-line antibiotic regimens
- **Low-risk outpatient CAP**: previously healthy patients without recent antibiotic use can be treated with **doxycycline 100 mg PO BID** or **amoxicillin 1 gm PO TID** [N3-R2].
- **Hospitalized patients**: the guidelines recommend **fluoroquinolone** or **beta-lactam plus macrolide** combinations [N3-R5].
- **General outpatient CAP**: outpatient CAP is often managed with shorter-course antibiotics once clinical stability is achieved [N6-R3].

### When to use combination therapy or broader coverage
- Use **combination therapy** or **broader coverage** when the patient is at higher risk of severe disease, when local resistance patterns suggest broader coverage is needed, or when the patient is hospitalized [N3-F3].
- Add **MRSA coverage** with **vancomycin or linezolid** if the patient has a history of MRSA or recent IV antibiotics/hospitalization [N8-R2].
- Add **Pseudomonas coverage** when appropriate, especially in patients with risk factors or when local epidemiology suggests it [N8-R2].

### How to adjust antibiotics based on comorbidities and severity
- Adjust antibiotics based on **clinical response** and **microbiological results** [N8-R1].
- For outpatients who reach clinical stability, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate, with a minimum of 3 days [N6-R3].
- For complicated pneumonia, therapy should continue for at least 2 weeks once fever is gone and may be extended for up to 4 weeks [N6-R1].
- If MRSA or Pseudomonas is confirmed, adjust duration accordingly [N8-R4].

### Key takeaway
Start with a guideline-based first-line regimen, use combination therapy when needed, and adjust based on severity, comorbidities, and response to treatment [N3-F3][N3-R5][N3-R2][N8-R2].

## 3) When to step up care and what escalation options are appropriate

The evidence supports a clear escalation logic: move from observation or outpatient treatment to hospitalization, ICU admission, or transfer when clinical deterioration, worsening respiratory failure, or failure to respond to treatment occurs.

### Clinical signs or lab findings that indicate escalation
- Shortness of breath, fever, and respiratory distress [N2-R3].
- Abnormal vital signs, especially respiratory failure and worsening respiratory status [N4-R3].
- Failure to improve after initial treatment [N2-R5][N6-R1].

### When to consider ICU admission or transfer
- Consider ICU admission if there is **worsening respiratory failure** or if the patient is at high risk of deterioration [N4-R3].
- Patients initially admitted to a non-ICU setting but later requiring ICU transfer have higher mortality than patients treated in the ICU [N4-R5].
- A pneumonia patient can be safely transferred from the ICU to the ward when they no longer meet severe CAP criteria and have achieved stability [N4-R4].

### How to decide between observation, outpatient treatment, or hospitalization
- Use outpatient care for stable, low-risk patients who meet mild disease criteria [N2-R1][N2-R3].
- Use hospitalization when there is concern about deterioration or when outpatient treatment fails [N2-R5][N4-R5].
- Use ICU admission when respiratory failure worsens or when the patient is at higher risk [N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 4) Practical implementation and limitations of the triage process

The triage process using severity scores like CRB-65 and CURB-65 is useful but not perfect. It works best when used alongside clinical judgment.

### Common pitfalls
- Over-reliance on the score alone can lead to incorrect decisions, especially in community settings [N1-F1].
- CURB-65 may over-predict 30-day mortality in community settings and should be used with caution [N1-F1].
- The score should be used to **supplement, not replace, clinical judgment** [N7-R5].

### How to handle uncertainty or atypical presentations
- Atypical presentations require more cautious escalation than the score alone would suggest [N7-R5].
- Clinical judgment must remain central, especially for patients whose presentation is unusual or does not fit a standard pattern [N7-R5][N4-R5].

### What to do if the patient is not improving after treatment
- If the patient is not improving, reassess treatment, consider changing antibiotics, and escalate care if needed [N6-R1][N8-R1].
- Approximately 10% of outpatients do not respond to antibiotic therapy and require hospitalization [N2-R5].
- Most patients respond to outpatient therapy for 5 to 7 days [N2-R3].

## 5) Follow-up and reassessment after pneumonia treatment

After treatment starts, follow-up should focus on monitoring improvement and determining whether treatment can be adjusted or escalated.

### What to monitor during follow-up
- Clinical improvement and fever clearance [N6-R1].
- Resolution of respiratory symptoms [N6-R2].
- Overall stability and response to treatment [N6-F4].

### When to repeat imaging or lab tests
- Repeat chest X-rays may be considered at 6 weeks after discharge in people with risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease, or when there are persisting symptoms [N6-R2].
- Reassess with safety assessment, medication management, and medical reevaluation after severe pneumonia or acute respiratory failure [N6-F4].

### When to reassess treatment and escalate care
- Reassess treatment if the patient is not improving [N6-R1][N2-R5].
- If clinical stability is reached, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate [N6-R3].
- If the patient is still unstable, consider changing antibiotics and escalating care [N8-R1].

## 6) Summary: quick patient-friendly steps

### Step 1: Triage using CRB-65 or CURB-65
- Use **CRB-65** for a quick, simple community rule [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- Use **CURB-65** for more detailed severity stratification when urea is available [N1-F2][N7-R4].
- Always use the score to **supplement clinical judgment**, not replace it [N7-R5].

### Step 2: Choose initial antibiotics
- Outpatient low-risk CAP: **doxycycline** or **amoxicillin** [N3-R2].
- Hospitalized CAP: **fluoroquinolone** or **beta-lactam plus macrolide** [N3-R5].
- Add broader coverage if there is MRSA, Pseudomonas, or other risk factors [N8-R2].

### Step 3: Step up care if needed
- Escalate if there is worsening respiratory failure, fever, shortness of breath, or failure to improve [N2-R3][N4-R3][N2-R5].
- Consider ICU admission if respiratory failure worsens or the patient is at high risk [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- Transfer from ICU to ward when the patient stabilizes and no longer meets severe CAP criteria [N4-R4].

### Step 4: Follow up and reassess
- Monitor clinical improvement and fever clearance [N6-R1].
- Repeat imaging or lab tests selectively if there are risk factors or persistent symptoms [N6-R2].
- Reassess treatment if the patient is not improving, and change antibiotics as needed [N6-R1][N8-R1].

If the patient is not improving after treatment, the evidence clearly says to **reassess treatment and escalate care** rather than continue the same regimen indefinitely [N6-R1][N8-R1]. The main takeaway is: **do not rely on a score alone; use it with clinical judgment, adjust antibiotics when needed, and escalate care when the patient is getting worse or not responding** [N1-F1][N7-R5][N2-R5].

## 1) Quick triage using CRB-65 and CURB-65

The two most commonly used severity scores for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) are **CRB-65** and **CURB-65**. Both are intended to help you decide whether the patient is likely to be stable enough for outpatient treatment or needs hospitalization, but they differ in what they measure and where they are best used.

### CRB-65
- **What it measures**: new-onset confusion, respiratory rate ≥30/min, systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≤60 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F1].
- **Why it matters**: CRB-65 is simpler and intended for community settings because it uses only clinical assessment and does not require laboratory testing such as urea [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- **Thresholds and risk groups**: the evidence says CRB-65 separates patients into low, intermediate, and high risk based on those four criteria [N1-F1]. The provided material does not give a single numerical cutoff for low-risk versus higher-risk, so the main point is that higher scores mean higher mortality risk [N1-F1].
- **Best when**: you want a quick, simple rule in community practice and laboratory testing is not readily available [N1-F1][N7-R3].

### CURB-65
- **What it measures**: confusion, urea >7 mmol/l, respiratory rate ≥30/min, blood pressure ≤90 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F2].
- **Why it matters**: CURB-65 is a five-point score that estimates mortality of CAP to help determine inpatient versus outpatient treatment [N1-F2].
- **Thresholds and risk groups**: the cutoffs are explicit: 0 or 1 = outpatient care; 2 = intermediate risk; ≥3 = inpatient admission with consideration for ICU admission for scores of 4 or 5 [N1-F2]. Higher scores also correlate with higher mortality [N1-R3].
- **Best when**: you need a more detailed severity stratification, urea can be measured, and you are in a setting where laboratory data are available [N1-F2][N7-R4].

### Practical difference
- **CRB-65** is simpler and better suited for community use [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- **CURB-65** is more sensitive for severe illness and better suited for hospital or settings where urea is available [N1-F2][N7-R4].
- Both scores should be used to **supplement, not replace, clinical judgment** [N7-R5].

## 2) How to choose initial antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia

The evidence points to a clear evidence-based approach: first-line antibiotics depend on the patient’s risk, severity, and local resistance patterns, but commonly include beta-lactam/macrolide combinations, fluoroquinolones, or other broad-cover regimens when needed.

### Recommended first-line antibiotic regimens
- **Low-risk outpatient CAP**: previously healthy patients without recent antibiotic use can be treated with **doxycycline 100 mg PO BID** or **amoxicillin 1 gm PO TID** [N3-R2].
- **Hospitalized patients**: the guidelines recommend **fluoroquinolone** or **beta-lactam plus macrolide** combinations [N3-R5].
- **General outpatient CAP**: outpatient CAP is often managed with shorter-course antibiotics once clinical stability is achieved [N6-R3].

### When to use combination therapy or broader coverage
- Use **combination therapy** or **broader coverage** when the patient is at higher risk of severe disease, when local resistance patterns suggest broader coverage is needed, or when the patient is hospitalized [N3-F3].
- Add **MRSA coverage** with **vancomycin or linezolid** if the patient has a history of MRSA or recent IV antibiotics/hospitalization [N8-R2].
- Add **Pseudomonas coverage** when appropriate, especially in patients with risk factors or when local epidemiology suggests it [N8-R2].

### How to adjust antibiotics based on comorbidities and severity
- Adjust antibiotics based on **clinical response** and **microbiological results** [N8-R1].
- For outpatients who reach clinical stability, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate, with a minimum of 3 days [N6-R3].
- For complicated pneumonia, therapy should continue for at least 2 weeks once fever is gone and may be extended for up to 4 weeks [N6-R1].
- If MRSA or Pseudomonas is confirmed, adjust duration accordingly [N8-R4].

### Key takeaway
Start with a guideline-based first-line regimen, use combination therapy when needed, and adjust based on severity, comorbidities, and response to treatment [N3-F3][N3-R5][N3-R2][N8-R2].

## 3) When to step up care and what escalation options are appropriate

The evidence supports a clear escalation logic: move from observation or outpatient treatment to hospitalization, ICU admission, or transfer when clinical deterioration, worsening respiratory failure, or failure to respond to treatment occurs.

### Clinical signs or lab findings that indicate escalation
- Shortness of breath, fever, and respiratory distress [N2-R3].
- Abnormal vital signs, especially respiratory failure and worsening respiratory status [N4-R3].
- Failure to improve after initial treatment [N2-R5][N6-R1].

### When to consider ICU admission or transfer
- Consider ICU admission if there is **worsening respiratory failure** or if the patient is at high risk of deterioration [N4-R3].
- Patients initially admitted to a non-ICU setting but later requiring ICU transfer have higher mortality than patients treated in the ICU [N4-R5].
- A pneumonia patient can be safely transferred from the ICU to the ward when they no longer meet severe CAP criteria and have achieved stability [N4-R4].

### How to decide between observation, outpatient treatment, or hospitalization
- Use outpatient care for stable, low-risk patients who meet mild disease criteria [N2-R1][N2-R3].
- Use hospitalization when there is concern about deterioration or when outpatient treatment fails [N2-R5][N4-R5].
- Use ICU admission when respiratory failure worsens or when the patient is at higher risk [N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 4) Practical implementation and limitations of the triage process

The triage process using severity scores like CRB-65 and CURB-65 is useful but not perfect. It works best when used alongside clinical judgment.

### Common pitfalls
- Over-reliance on the score alone can lead to incorrect decisions, especially in community settings [N1-F1].
- CURB-65 may over-predict 30-day mortality in community settings and should be used with caution [N1-F1].
- The score should be used to **supplement, not replace, clinical judgment** [N7-R5].

### How to handle uncertainty or atypical presentations
- Atypical presentations require more cautious escalation than the score alone would suggest [N7-R5].
- Clinical judgment must remain central, especially for patients whose presentation is unusual or does not fit a standard pattern [N7-R5][N4-R5].

### What to do if the patient is not improving after treatment
- If the patient is not improving, reassess treatment, consider changing antibiotics, and escalate care if needed [N6-R1][N8-R1].
- Approximately 10% of outpatients do not respond to antibiotic therapy and require hospitalization [N2-R5].
- Most patients respond to outpatient therapy for 5 to 7 days [N2-R3].

## 5) Follow-up and reassessment after pneumonia treatment

After treatment starts, follow-up should focus on monitoring improvement and determining whether treatment can be adjusted or escalated.

### What to monitor during follow-up
- Clinical improvement and fever clearance [N6-R1].
- Resolution of respiratory symptoms [N6-R2].
- Overall stability and response to treatment [N6-F4].

### When to repeat imaging or lab tests
- Repeat chest X-rays may be considered at 6 weeks after discharge in people with risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease, or when there are persisting symptoms [N6-R2].
- Reassess with safety assessment, medication management, and medical reevaluation after severe pneumonia or acute respiratory failure [N6-F4].

### When to reassess treatment and escalate care
- Reassess treatment if the patient is not improving [N6-R1][N2-R5].
- If clinical stability is reached, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate [N6-R3].
- If the patient is still unstable, consider changing antibiotics and escalating care [N8-R1].

## 6) Summary: quick patient-friendly steps

### Step 1: Triage using CRB-65 or CURB-65
- Use **CRB-65** for a quick, simple community rule [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- Use **CURB-65** for more detailed severity stratification when urea is available [N1-F2][N7-R4].
- Always use the score to **supplement clinical judgment**, not replace it [N7-R5].

### Step 2: Choose initial antibiotics
- Outpatient low-risk CAP: **doxycycline** or **amoxicillin** [N3-R2].
- Hospitalized CAP: **fluoroquinolone** or **beta-lactam plus macrolide** [N3-R5].
- Add broader coverage if there is MRSA, Pseudomonas, or other risk factors [N8-R2].
- Adjust duration and regimen based on clinical response and microbiological results [N8-R1][N6-R3].

### Step 3: Step up care if needed
- Escalate if there is worsening respiratory failure, fever, shortness of breath, or failure to improve [N2-R3][N4-R3][N2-R5].
- Consider ICU admission if respiratory failure worsens or the patient is at high risk [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- Transfer from ICU to ward when the patient stabilizes and no longer meets severe CAP criteria [N4-R4].

### Step 4: Follow up and reassess
- Monitor clinical improvement and fever clearance [N6-R1].
- Repeat imaging or lab tests selectively if there are risk factors or persistent symptoms [N6-R2].
- Reassess treatment if the patient is not improving, and change antibiotics as needed [N6-R1][N8-R1].

## Final practical note

If the patient is not improving after treatment, the evidence clearly says to **reassess treatment and escalate care** rather than continue the same regimen indefinitely [N6-R1][N8-R1]. The main takeaway is: **do not rely on a score alone; use it with clinical judgment, adjust antibiotics when needed, and escalate care when the patient is getting worse or not responding** [N1-F1][N7-R5][N2-R5].

# Integrated final answer: how to quickly triage pneumonia using CRB-65 or CURB-65, pick antibiotics, and step up care if needed

## 1) Quick triage using CRB-65 and CURB-65

The two most commonly used severity scores for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) are **CRB-65** and **CURB-65**. Both are intended to help you decide whether the patient is likely to be stable enough for outpatient treatment or needs hospitalization, but they differ in what they measure and where they are best used.

### CRB-65
- **What it measures**: new-onset confusion, respiratory rate ≥30/min, systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≤60 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F1].
- **Why it matters**: CRB-65 is simpler and intended for community settings because it uses only clinical assessment and does not require laboratory testing such as urea [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- **Thresholds and risk groups**: the evidence says CRB-65 separates patients into low, intermediate, and high risk based on those four criteria [N1-F1]. The provided material does not give a single numerical cutoff for low-risk versus higher-risk, so the main point is that higher scores mean higher mortality risk [N1-F1].
- **Best when**: you want a quick, simple rule in community practice and laboratory testing is not readily available [N1-F1][N7-R3].

### CURB-65
- **What it measures**: confusion, urea >7 mmol/l, respiratory rate ≥30/min, blood pressure ≤90 mmHg, and age ≥65 years [N1-F2].
- **Why it matters**: CURB-65 is a five-point score that estimates mortality of CAP to help determine inpatient versus outpatient treatment [N1-F2].
- **Thresholds and risk groups**: the cutoffs are explicit: 0 or 1 = outpatient care; 2 = intermediate risk; ≥3 = inpatient admission with consideration for ICU admission for scores of 4 or 5 [N1-F2]. Higher scores also correlate with higher mortality [N1-R3].
- **Best when**: you need a more detailed severity stratification, urea can be measured, and you are in a setting where laboratory data are available [N1-F2][N7-R4].

### Practical difference
- **CRB-65** is simpler and better suited for community use [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- **CURB-65** is more sensitive for severe illness and better suited for hospital or settings where urea is available [N1-F2][N7-R4].
- Both scores should be used to **supplement, not replace, clinical judgment** [N7-R5].

## 2) How to choose initial antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia

The evidence points to a clear evidence-based approach: first-line antibiotics depend on the patient’s risk, severity, and local resistance patterns, but commonly include beta-lactam/macrolide combinations, fluoroquinolones, or other broad-cover regimens when needed.

### Recommended first-line antibiotic regimens
- **Low-risk outpatient CAP**: previously healthy patients without recent antibiotic use can be treated with **doxycycline 100 mg PO BID** or **amoxicillin 1 gm PO TID** [N3-R2].
- **Hospitalized patients**: the guidelines recommend **fluoroquinolone** or **beta-lactam plus macrolide** combinations [N3-R5].
- **General outpatient CAP**: outpatient CAP is often managed with shorter-course antibiotics once clinical stability is achieved [N6-R3].

### When to use combination therapy or broader coverage
- Use **combination therapy** or **broader coverage** when the patient is at higher risk of severe disease, when local resistance patterns suggest broader coverage is needed, or when the patient is hospitalized [N3-F3].
- Add **MRSA coverage** with **vancomycin or linezolid** if the patient has a history of MRSA or recent IV antibiotics/hospitalization [N8-R2].
- Add **Pseudomonas coverage** when appropriate, especially in patients with risk factors or when local epidemiology suggests it [N8-R2].

### How to adjust antibiotics based on comorbidities and severity
- Adjust antibiotics based on **clinical response** and **microbiological results** [N8-R1].
- For outpatients who reach clinical stability, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate, with a minimum of 3 days [N6-R3].
- For complicated pneumonia, therapy should continue for at least 2 weeks once fever is gone and may be extended for up to 4 weeks [N6-R1].
- If MRSA or Pseudomonas is confirmed, adjust duration accordingly [N8-R4].

### Key takeaway
Start with a guideline-based first-line regimen, use combination therapy when needed, and adjust based on severity, comorbidities, and response to treatment [N3-F3][N3-R5][N3-R2][N8-R2].

## 3) When to step up care and what escalation options are appropriate

The evidence supports a clear escalation logic: move from observation or outpatient treatment to hospitalization, ICU admission, or transfer when clinical deterioration, worsening respiratory failure, or failure to respond to treatment occurs.

### Clinical signs or lab findings that indicate escalation
- Shortness of breath, fever, and respiratory distress [N2-R3].
- Abnormal vital signs, especially respiratory failure and worsening respiratory status [N4-R3].
- Failure to improve after initial treatment [N2-R5][N6-R1].

### When to consider ICU admission or transfer
- Consider ICU admission if there is **worsening respiratory failure** or if the patient is at high risk of deterioration [N4-R3].
- Patients initially admitted to a non-ICU setting but later requiring ICU transfer have higher mortality than patients treated in the ICU [N4-R5].
- A pneumonia patient can be safely transferred from the ICU to the ward when they no longer meet severe CAP criteria and have achieved stability [N4-R4].

### How to decide between observation, outpatient treatment, or hospitalization
- Use outpatient care for stable, low-risk patients who meet mild disease criteria [N2-R1][N2-R3].
- Use hospitalization when there is concern about deterioration or when outpatient treatment fails [N2-R5][N4-R5].
- Use ICU admission when respiratory failure worsens or when the patient is at higher risk [N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 4) Practical implementation and limitations of the triage process

The triage process using severity scores like CRB-65 and CURB-65 is useful but not perfect. It works best when used alongside clinical judgment.

### Common pitfalls
- Over-reliance on the score alone can lead to incorrect decisions, especially in community settings [N1-F1].
- CURB-65 may over-predict 30-day mortality in community settings and should be used with caution [N1-F1].
- The score should be used to **supplement, not replace, clinical judgment** [N7-R5].

### How to handle uncertainty or atypical presentations
- Atypical presentations require more cautious escalation than the score alone would suggest [N7-R5].
- Clinical judgment must remain central, especially for patients whose presentation is unusual or does not fit a standard pattern [N7-R5][N4-R5].

### What to do if the patient is not improving after treatment
- If the patient is not improving, reassess treatment, consider changing antibiotics, and escalate care if needed [N6-R1][N8-R1].
- Approximately 10% of outpatients do not respond to antibiotic therapy and require hospitalization [N2-R5].
- Most patients respond to outpatient therapy for 5 to 7 days [N2-R3].

## 5) Follow-up and reassessment after pneumonia treatment

After treatment starts, follow-up should focus on monitoring improvement and determining whether treatment can be adjusted or escalated.

### What to monitor during follow-up
- Clinical improvement and fever clearance [N6-R1].
- Resolution of respiratory symptoms [N6-R2].
- Overall stability and response to treatment [N6-F4].

### When to repeat imaging or lab tests
- Repeat chest X-rays may be considered at 6 weeks after discharge in people with risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease, or when there are persisting symptoms [N6-R2].
- Reassess with safety assessment, medication management, and medical reevaluation after severe pneumonia or acute respiratory failure [N6-F4].

### When to reassess treatment and escalate care
- Reassess treatment if the patient is not improving [N6-R1][N2-R5].
- If clinical stability is reached, shorter antibiotic duration may be appropriate [N6-R3].
- If the patient is still unstable, consider changing antibiotics and escalating care [N8-R1].

## 6) Summary: quick patient-friendly steps

### Step 1: Triage using CRB-65 or CURB-65
- Use **CRB-65** for a quick, simple community rule [N1-F1][N7-R3].
- Use **CURB-65** for more detailed severity stratification when urea is available [N1-F2][N7-R4].
- Always use the score to **supplement clinical judgment**, not replace it [N7-R5].

### Step 2: Choose initial antibiotics
- Outpatient low-risk CAP: **doxycycline** or **amoxicillin** [N3-R2].
- Hospitalized CAP: **fluoroquinolone** or **beta-lactam plus macrolide** [N3-R5].
- Add broader coverage if there is MRSA, Pseudomonas, or other risk factors [N8-R2].
- Adjust duration and regimen based on clinical response and microbiological results [N8-R1][N6-R3].

### Step 3: Step up care if needed
- Escalate if there is worsening respiratory failure, fever, shortness of breath, or failure to improve [N2-R3][N4-R3][N2-R5].
- Consider ICU admission if respiratory failure worsens or the patient is at high risk [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- Transfer from ICU to ward when the patient stabilizes and no longer meets severe CAP criteria [N4-R4].

### Step 4: Follow up and reassess
- Monitor clinical improvement and fever clearance [N6-R1].
- Repeat imaging or lab tests selectively if there are risk factors or persistent symptoms [N6-R2].
- Reassess treatment if the patient is not improving, and change antibiotics as needed [N6-R1][N8-R1].

## Final practical note

If the patient is not improving after treatment, the evidence clearly says to **reassess treatment and escalate care** rather than continue the same regimen indefinitely [N6-R1][N8-R1]. The main takeaway is: **do not rely on a score alone; use it with clinical judgment, adjust antibiotics when needed, and escalate care when the patient is getting worse or not responding** [N1-F1][N7-R5][N2-R5].
